narrative: The model estimated a 55% probability that you would fail the bar exam on the first attempt. That is only slightly above a coin flip, but it was enough for the review process to treat your application as too risky and deny admission. The decisive factor was your LSAT score of 26, which is far below the average of about 37 among accepted students and was the strongest influence pushing the prediction toward failure. The next most important factor was your high family-income bracket; in this model it worked mildly in your favor, toward passing. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.80 was the third most influential factor and also leaned toward passing, even though it is below the accepted average of 3.23. Together, those favorable signals were not strong enough to offset the LSAT concern. Because the estimate is close to 50%, this looks more like a borderline risk flag than a certainty. To strengthen a future application, focus first on raising your LSAT score through structured preparation and a retake if feasible. Also consider meeting with admissions to ask what academic evidence would reduce the concern, and consider applying after additional coursework or work experience that demonstrates readiness.
